meta.title: Who really said "Whether you think you can or you think you can't, you're right"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Henry Ford almost certainly never said it. The line was pinned to him in Reader's Digest five months after he died — the idea goes back to Virgil.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Whether you think you can or you think you can't, you're right'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Henry Ford. First credited to him posthumously in 1947 with no source; the idea traces to Virgil and the exact wording predates the attribution.

answer.label: Not Henry Ford — an anonymous proverb pinned to him after his death
answer.authorDates: American folk saying — documented in this ‘you’re right’ form by 1940; roots in Virgil, c. 19 BC
answer.sourceLine: There is no evidence Henry Ford ever said or wrote this. The saying was first attached to Ford — as “Whether you believe you can do a thing or not, you are right” — in The Reader’s Digest of September 1947 ↗, five months after Ford died and with no source given. The idea is far older, and the exact “you’re right” wording is documented before any Ford attribution.

source.excerpt: Whether you think you can or you think you can’t, you’re right.
trail: c. 19 BC — Virgil’s Aeneid carries the seed idea, rendered by Dryden (1697) as “For they can conquer who believe they can ↗.”
1914 — baseball manager Del Howard: “If you think you can, you can. If you think you can’t, you can’t,” per Quote Investigator ↗.
Sept 1947 — The Reader’s Digest ↗ prints it under Ford’s name for the first time, months after his death, with no source.
Today — Wikiquote editors place it among Ford’s unverified / posthumous attributions ↗, not his sourced quotations.
source.cutTag: ↑ the wording Ford was actually given in 1947 differs from the popular version
source.excerptNote: The most-shared modern form. The version actually printed under Ford’s name in 1947 was slightly different: “Whether you believe you can do a thing or not, you are right.” The crisp “you’re right” ending is documented earlier — e.g. a 1940 Iowa State locker-room sign: “If you think you can, you can; if you think you can’t, you’re right.”

source.rightsNote: Short proverbial phrases are not protected by copyright, and this saying’s underlying idea is centuries old (Virgil, Dryden). Freely quotable; just don’t credit it to Henry Ford as fact.

author.name: Anonymous (traditional proverb)
author.heading: About Anonymous (traditional proverb)
author.metaLine: American motivational saying · documented by 1940 · idea from Virgil, c. 19 BC
author.bio: This is a folk aphorism with no single verifiable author. Its core idea — that belief determines outcome — runs from Virgil’s Aeneid (“they can because they think they can”) through John Dryden’s 1697 translation into American motivational and sporting culture, where the sharp “you’re right” form circulated in the 1910s–1940s. It was welded to Henry Ford only in 1947, after his death, and has traveled under his name ever since.

cite.sourceCitation: Earliest documented Ford attribution: a filler item in The Reader’s Digest, September 1947 (Vol. 51, p. 64), as traced in Garson O’Toole, “Whether You Believe You Can Do a Thing or Not, You Are Right,” Quote Investigator, February 3, 2015.

misattribution.heading: The Henry Ford problem
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most confidently misattributed lines on the internet — hundreds of books and countless posters credit it to Henry Ford. The documentary record does not support that.

items.why: Ford died in April 1947. The saying was first printed under his name in The Reader’s Digest of September 1947 ↗ — five months later — with no source, and no Ford speech, letter, or book has ever been found containing it. Wikiquote editors keep it out of his sourced quotations ↗.

items.who: Robert H. Schuller, Norman Vincent Peale & Mary Kay Ash
items.why: Schuller (1973) re-attributed a variant to Ford; Peale used a version but credited a friend, Harlowe B. Andrews; Mary Kay Ash (1985) credited Peale — per Quote Investigator ↗. The tangle of credits is itself evidence no one can point to an original.

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: the idea is Virgil’s, the wording is anonymous American folk-motivation, and the Ford credit is a posthumous 1947 accident ↗ that stuck.

context.heading: Why it stuck to Ford
lead: Henry Ford was the perfect magnet for a can-do aphorism: the self-taught mechanic who built an empire on the conviction that ordinary problems could be engineered away. A line about belief determining outcome sounds like him — which is exactly how misattributions harden into ‘facts.’

But the paper trail points elsewhere. The thought is ancient (Virgil’s “possunt quia posse videntur”), and the punchy English version circulated in sports and pep-talk culture for decades before a 1947 magazine put Ford’s name on it.
context.detailsSummary: The chain of wording, from Virgil to the locker room
detailsBody: Dryden’s 1697 Aeneid gave English “For they can conquer who believe they can.” By 1914 a baseball manager, Del Howard, was saying “If you think you can, you can. If you think you can’t, you can’t.”

The exact modern ending appears on a 1940 Iowa State football locker-room sign: “If you think you can, you can; if you think you can’t, you’re right” — a full seven years before Reader’s Digest attached the sentiment to Henry Ford.
context.pull: The idea is Virgil’s. The wording is anonymous. Only the credit is Ford’s — and even that came after he died.
